--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Work Breakdown Structures (WBS) ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Explain** what a WBS is and how it links scope, schedule, and budget. 2. **Decompose** a project into deliverables, work packages, and activities. 3. **Apply** the 100 % rule, the mutually-exclusive rule, and "plan outcomes, not actions." 4. **Choose** an appropriate level of decomposition using the 8/80 and single-reporting-period rules of thumb. 5. **Number** a WBS and write a WBS dictionary entry for a work package. 6. **Roll up** cost and effort from work packages to the total project. 7. **State** the six requirements of a valid project contract and the purpose of work authorization.
Before we begin: how do you eat an elephant? One bite at a time. *"Project managers cannot manage projects. Project managers manage pieces of projects."* The WBS is how you cut the elephant into bites.
## Introduction: from a scope statement to something you can manage You have a signed scope statement for the RC-vehicle replica. It is still far too big to schedule, budget, or assign. The **work breakdown structure** is the bridge: it takes the total scope and breaks it into **deliverables**, then **work packages**, then **activities** small enough that one person can own each one and you can put a real number on it. > **Definition.** A WBS is a **deliverable-oriented** grouping of project > components that organizes and defines the **total scope** of the project. A well-built WBS lets the team **plan every step**, **collect and organize** the information each task needs, and **assign** manageable chunks to team members. It also enables the **WBS dictionary**, which pins down the requirements for each task. ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** An automotive program WBS separates *body*, *powertrain integration*, *electrical*, *validation*, and *launch* --- each a deliverable, not an action. A food-plant install WBS breaks out *utilities*, *process equipment*, *controls*, *sanitation qualification*, and *commissioning*. A defense contract WBS follows a mandated standard (MIL-STD-881) so the customer can track cost against the exact same structure the contractor uses. :::
## The hierarchy ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The `label.size` argument of `geom_label()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.5.0. ℹ Please use the `linewidth` argument instead. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A partial WBS for the RC-vehicle project. Level 1 is the project; Level 2 the major deliverables; Level 3 the work packages. Numbering encodes the hierarchy.](05-Work-Breakdown-Structures_files/figure-epub/fig-wbs-tree-05-1.png){#fig-wbs-tree-05 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: - **Level 1** --- the project. *What is the project?* - **Level 2** --- the summary level: the project's major deliverables. - **Level 3** --- the start of the **work package** level (more levels if the package is complex). The same content can be shown as a **tree** (good for communicating structure) or a **tabular / indented list** (good for working). Both carry the numbering. ## Design principles ### The 100 % rule The WBS includes **100 % of the work** in the scope --- all deliverables, internal, external, and interim --- and **no more**. At every level, the **sum of the children equals the parent**, and nothing outside the scope appears. ### Worked Example 1: does this WBS roll up to 100 %? The "1.1 Body & Frame" deliverable is estimated at **340 hours**. Its four work packages are estimated at 120, 90, 70, and 60 hours. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parent_hours <- 340 children_hours <- c("1.1.1 Outer body design" = 120, "1.1.2 Inner frame design" = 90, "1.1.3 Material selection" = 70, "1.1.4 Design review & release" = 60) child_sum <- sum(children_hours) cat("Children:\n"); print(children_hours) cat(sprintf("\nSum of children : %d h\n", child_sum)) cat(sprintf("Parent estimate : %d h\n", parent_hours)) if (child_sum == parent_hours) { cat("OK - the children account for exactly 100% of the parent.\n") } else if (child_sum < parent_hours) { cat(sprintf("GAP - %d h of the parent's scope is not captured by any work package.\n", parent_hours - child_sum)) } else { cat(sprintf("OVER - the children exceed the parent by %d h (>100%% -- scope crept in).\n", child_sum - parent_hours)) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Children: 1.1.1 Outer body design 1.1.2 Inner frame design 120 90 1.1.3 Material selection 1.1.4 Design review & release 70 60 Sum of children : 340 h Parent estimate : 340 h OK - the children account for exactly 100% of the parent. ``` ::: ::: Here the children sum to 340 --- the deliverable is fully decomposed with nothing missing and nothing extra. ### Mutually exclusive **No overlap** between WBS elements. Overlap causes duplicated work, confusion over who is responsible, and messy cost accounting. If element names are ambiguous, the **WBS dictionary** disambiguates them. ### Plan outcomes, not actions Define elements as **results** ("Training module completed"), not **actions** ("write script", "record video", "upload"). Action lists always capture too many or too few steps --- breaking the 100 % rule --- and they over-prescribe *how* the work is done, killing the team's ingenuity. ## Level of detail A work package at the **activity level** is a task that: - can be **realistically and confidently estimated**; - makes no practical sense to break down further; - produces a **measurable deliverable**; and - forms a unique package that **could be outsourced or contracted out**. **Rules of thumb for how far to decompose:** - **80-hour rule** --- no work package (single deliverable at the lowest level) exceeds ~80 hours of effort. - **One reporting period** --- no package is longer than a single progress-reporting period (if you report monthly, nothing runs longer than a month). - **8-hour floor** --- generally do not define a task below ~8 hours; below that you are micromanaging. - **"If it makes sense"** --- apply common sense. ### Try it yourself: decomposition check ```{webr-r} #| label: wbs-decomp-05 packages <- data.frame( id = c("1.1.1", "1.2.1", "1.3.1", "1.3.4", "1.4.2"), name = c("Outer body design", "Motor/controller procurement", "Prototype assembly", "Tighten one fastener", "Full regulatory approval campaign"), hours = c(64, 40, 72, 1.5, 260) ) flag <- ifelse(packages$hours > 80, "TOO BIG (> 80 h -- split it)", ifelse(packages$hours < 8, "TOO SMALL (< 8 h -- roll it up)", "ok")) out <- cbind(packages, verdict = flag) print(out, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d packages need re-sizing.\n", sum(flag != "ok"), nrow(packages))) ``` ## Why the WBS matters ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The WBS feeds four downstream planning activities. Get it wrong and the estimate, the schedule, the staffing plan, and the risk register are all built on sand.](05-Work-Breakdown-Structures_files/figure-epub/fig-wbs-hub-05-1.png){#fig-wbs-hub-05 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ## The WBS dictionary The dictionary is used to **control what work is done and when**, **prevent scope creep**, and **capture the effort** for each task. Physically, teams post the work packages on a wall in logical work-flow order; **removing them in numerical order generates the dictionary**. Each entry --- a **task description** --- records: - Task description (what work is authorized) - Quantified objectives and deliverables (cross-referenced to the charter) - Product description; acceptance criteria (how the owner checks their own work) - Assumptions; resources assigned; duration; cost; due date - Interdependencies (before this task / after this task) - Project manager approval and date ## Work authorization and contracts Once the scope is decomposed into work packages, stakeholders formally agree on project content --- the **work authorization**. If the client is external, this includes the **contract sign-off**. A valid project-management contract requires all six of: 1. The legal **right** to contract 2. Legal **age** (18 in Ontario and Quebec; 19 or 21 elsewhere in Canada) 3. **Sound mind** at signing 4. Valid, legal **consideration** for both parties 5. A **legal scope of work** 6. **Offer and acceptance** Contracts also commonly contain: excusable delays; allowable costs; **liquidated damages** (non-performance / penalty clauses); inspection criteria; responsibility for correcting defects; and dispute-resolution mechanisms. ### Try it yourself: cost roll-up from the WBS ```{webr-r} #| label: wbs-cost-rollup-05 # Work-package costs (direct), grouped by Level-2 deliverable. wp <- data.frame( deliverable = c(rep("1.1 Body & Frame", 3), rep("1.2 Drive & Controls", 2), rep("1.3 Assembly & Test", 3), rep("1.4 Launch", 2)), package = c("Outer body", "Inner frame", "Material selection", "Motor/controller", "Wiring harness", "Prototype assembly", "Drop test", "EMC test", "Packaging design", "Approvals"), cost = c(18000, 14000, 6000, 140000, 9000, 21000, 12000, 15000, 8000, 6000) ) by_deliverable <- tapply(wp$cost, wp$deliverable, sum) cat("Roll-up to Level 2:\n") for (d in names(by_deliverable)) cat(sprintf(" %-22s $%s\n", d, format(by_deliverable[d], big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("\nLevel 1 (total project direct cost): $%s\n", format(sum(wp$cost), big.mark = " "))) cat("\nThis roll-up only works because the WBS obeys the 100% and\n") cat("mutually-exclusive rules -- every dollar is counted once, and all of them.\n") ``` ## Key Takeaways - A **WBS** is a **deliverable-oriented** decomposition of the **total scope** into deliverables → work packages → activities. PMs manage the pieces. - **Numbering** encodes the hierarchy: Level 1 project, Level 2 deliverables, Level 3+ work packages. - Obey the three design rules: **100 % rule** (children sum to the parent, never more), **mutually exclusive** (no overlap), and **plan outcomes, not actions**. - Size work packages with the **8/80 rule** and the **one-reporting-period** rule; below ~8 h you are micromanaging, above ~80 h you cannot estimate confidently. - The WBS feeds **estimating, scheduling, staffing, and risk** --- errors propagate to all four. - The **WBS dictionary** locks down each task's description, acceptance criteria, resources, and interdependencies, and helps prevent scope creep. - **Work authorization** formalizes agreement on content; a valid contract needs all **six** legal elements and usually carries **liquidated-damages** and dispute clauses. ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Fix the 100 % rule violation The "1.3 Assembly & Test" deliverable is estimated at 300 h. Its packages are listed as: Prototype assembly (110 h), Drop test (60 h), EMC test (70 h), Prototype assembly rework (40 h), Write the test report (30 h), *and* "General project management (50 h)." What is wrong, and how do you fix it? **Solution.** The children sum to 360 h --- 60 h **over** 100 % of the parent. Two problems: "Prototype assembly rework" overlaps "Prototype assembly" (not mutually exclusive --- fold rework into the assembly package or make it a contingency), and "General project management" is **not part of this deliverable's scope** --- PM effort belongs in its own Level-2 element (e.g. "1.0.1 Project Management"), not smuggled into a technical deliverable.
Problem 2: Outcome or action? Rewrite these action-style entries as outcome-style WBS elements: 1. "Call three carbon-fibre suppliers and get quotes" 2. "Run the mould 20 times and measure the parts" 3. "Email the drawings to the customer for approval" **Model answers.** 1 → "Carbon-fibre supplier selected and quoted." 2 → "Moulding process capability established." 3 → "Customer design approval obtained." Each is a result you can mark done or not done, and it does not dictate the method.
Problem 3 (discussion): how deep should the RC-vehicle WBS go? Your draft WBS has a work package "Design the outer body" estimated at 180 h and spanning 6 weeks, and another, "Deburr the frame jig", estimated at 2 h. Using the rules of thumb, what do you do with each? **Discussion points.** "Design the outer body" breaks both the 80-hour rule and (if you report every 2 weeks) the single-reporting-period rule --- split it into concept, detailed CAD, and design-release packages. "Deburr the frame jig" is below the 8-hour floor --- roll it into the jig-fabrication package rather than tracking it as its own line.
